subsubtopic: KEABLE INQUIRY-MINISTER'S AFFIDAVIT RESPECTING DOCUMENTS NOT PROVIDED TO INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Solicitor General. Yesterday, I asked the minister specific questions about the state of knowledge of the previous solicitor general when he signed an affidavit on September 15 and, indeed, a subsequent affidavit on October 12, relating to the 26 documents which the solicitor general refused to turn over to the Keable inquiry. The Acting Solicitor General said his predecessor would not have known that one or more of those documents referred to operation "Ham", that is, the PQ break-in, because they were coded numerically.
Would the Acting Solicitor General explain to the House why the department, the security service or whoever it was, would use code numbers, when this operation had already been given a code name, namely, operation "Ham"?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: KEABLE INQUIRY-MINISTER'S AFFIDAVIT RESPECTING DOCUMENTS NOT PROVIDED TO INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity, which I appreciate the House giving me, of reviewing the annex to the affidavit to which the hon. member refers. There are three references to documents with references to file numbers. They were considered, along with the other 23 documents, by the then solicitor general against a set of criteria drawn up by him, his advisers and counsel- including counsel from my department-as to the basis upon which they should be excluded. Those three references had file references which later turned out to be references to the "Ham" file. I have reviewed the three documents which are excluded, and none of those documents, while they have a file reference, include the word "Ham".

February 1, 1978
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: KEABLE INQUIRY-MINISTER'S AFFIDAVIT RESPECTING DOCUMENTS NOT PROVIDED TO INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister indicated yesterday in his answers that there was no contradiction. In his answer on Monday, he said:
Any minister signing a section 41 declaration does so after careful examination of the documents in front of him-
Therefore, the very unfortunate question has to be: On October 28 or October 31, did the then solicitor general mislead the House; or on September 15 or October 12, did the then solicitor general sign a false affidavit?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: KEABLE INQUIRY-MINISTER'S AFFIDAVIT RESPECTING DOCUMENTS NOT PROVIDED TO INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to both those questions is an emphatic "No". The documents which were given to the Keable inquiry under that affidavit, and the documents that were withheld, were carefully reviewed by the then solicitor general, over some 70 hours of work with his advisers, as to which would be submitted to the inquiry and which would not. None of those documents refer to "Ham". Those 26 documents were excluded, on the basis of section 41(2), against a set of criteria including such things as the protection of human sources, technical sources, information from other security services and the revealing of other targets or operations of the RCMP.
At that time, the then solicitor general, in reviewing those documents, was reviewing documents relative to the Bricole file or the Bricole matter, the break-in at the APLQ, and was excluding documents which did not relate to that incident.

subsubtopic: KEABLE INQUIRY-MINISTER'S AFFIDAVIT RESPECTING DOCUMENTS NOT PROVIDED TO INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because this discussion is not clarifying anything, my final supplementary question is: Were there documents listed among the 26 which referred to activities other than those to which the affidavit referred, because the matters deposed to and the documents referred to in the affidavit related to specific events, being the subject matter of the inquiry of Mr. Justice Keable, specifically? Were these other three documents related to other activities, specifically, the Parti Quebecois break-in? How on earth could the minister fail to inform himself of that very situation, having, as his successor has said, met the standard of conduct required by a minister in signing a section 41 affidavit, which was outlined to the House by the Acting Solicitor General yesterday?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: KEABLE INQUIRY-MINISTER'S AFFIDAVIT RESPECTING DOCUMENTS NOT PROVIDED TO INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, they were documents which did not relate to the APLQ break-in, they related to other files of the RCMP which did not relate to the APLQ, and therefore were excluded from the affidavit relating to the APLQ. I think some of the confusion-and I indicated the other day that there is confusion-may well arise from the fact that there is in the annex, the list of excluded documents, a reference to a telex which does not use the word "Ham". There is, however, another telex of the same date, from the same officer which does refer to operation "Ham". That is not the telegram referred to in the annex, nor is it the document excluded by the former solicitor general.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. In view of the fact that the Alcan company is shutting down its fluorspar mine in St. Lawrence, Newfoundland-a criminal act which will throw 400 people in the community out of work-and in view of the fact that Alcan is doing this because they feel they can make more profit from the fluorspar mine owned by Noranda in Mexico, and in view of the fact that Alcan is brutalizing the community in this way, immediately following a year in which that company's profits increased by 500 per cent over the previous year, can the Acting Prime Minister tell the House why he refuses to protect the jobs of Canadians and the community of St. Lawrence by imposing temporary import tariffs on fluorspar?

Mir. Adrien Lambert (Bellechasse): Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport.
I have been told that over similar distances domestic rates differ from rates on overseas flights originating in Canada.
Could the minister tell the House whether those allegations are correct and, if so, what criteria are considered in establishing passenger rates inside or outside the country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN DOMESTIC AND OVERSEAS RATES- CRITERIA USED TO ESTABLISH RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to make a sweeping statement about a comparison of rates of all kinds within the country and abroad. However, it may be that the hon. member's question is directly related to a recent report of a higher rate between points in eastern Canada and Vancouver, compared with a lower rate if one is travelling to Los Angeles. That report, as an Air Canada vice president made clear in a letter to the same newspaper, was quite wrong. As usual, a charter economy or excursion fare was being compared with a regular fare inside Canada.
In fact, a real comparison of rates shows that the lowest rates generally available are charter competitive fares, which both CP Air and Air Canada offer. As that vice president reported, on the particular routes being used as the examples when comparing those two fares, the fare for the inside Canada route was actually lower than the one to the foreign destination.

subsubtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN DOMESTIC AND OVERSEAS RATES- CRITERIA USED TO ESTABLISH RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would the minister give serious attention to this matter, which is of great interest for all Canadians, so that people who wish to take a few days' vacation be better informed, and see if it might be possible to give a special advantage to Canadians who want to visit Canada rather than foreign countries?
Could the minister inform the House about this study? Would he be prepared to make that recommendation or to give the results of this study in the House of Commons within the next few days?

subsubtopic: DISINTEGRATION OF SOVIET SATELLITE OVER CANADIAN SOIL-INFORMATION PROVIDED MINISTER ON MILITARY MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. Has the minister discussed with the Prime Minister the advantages of keeping the minister informed about military matters? In turn, the minister might enlighten the Prime Minister regarding the role of NORAD.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: Order, please. It is my understanding that at the conclusion of the debate last evening, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) had the floor. Is the House ready for the question?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity in committee and through the debates in the House to take a good look at the bill before the House. It is such a short bill which contains so little that one could easily overlook its true significance. The significance of the bill is that the minister will have authority to increase to a large extent the fee structure for fishermen on the east and west coasts. We in this party are not opposed to rationalization of the small harbours system and we are not opposed to ending the idea that a fisherman can tie up at one wharf for nothing but at another wharf he has to pay the wharfinger.
I know that the minister is attempting through this legislation to solve this kind of inequity, but there are some real reasons for which we feel as a matter of principle we cannot support the bill. One of the fundamental principles which we in this party support is that one should not take the public's property and turn it over to the private sector and leave those in the fishing industry unprotected. Under section 8 this bill contains the clear provision that the minister may, subject to the regulations, lease any scheduled harbour or any part thereof to any person. First of all, I see nothing in this bill which would protect fishermen against moorage fees, which may amount to whatever the traffic can bear as far as the private lessee of that marina is concerned, or nothing to prevent the lessee deciding he does not want fishermen on his docks but just wants big yachts, because obviously he can make more money from yachts. I see the minister shaking his head and I hope he will correct us.
I do not see anything in the bill which guarantees that if the minister decides, under the powers of this legislation, to transfer a public small harbour to the private sector, fishermen will be protected in terms of the regulated fee under the act. I cannot imagine any private entrepreneur taking it on that basis without some flexibility in terms of the kinds of fees that a private entrepreneur would take.
What is really passing strange in this bill appears when one reads the record of evidence in committee and the statements made by the minister in the House about the whole question of the fee structure. On November 15, as recorded at page 2:5 of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, Mr. Reid, who looks after the small harbours division in the minister's department, said the following:
February 1, 1978

Some fishermen pay and others are not paying, depending on whether or not there is a government wharfinger to collect the charges. In fact, we have a number of outstanding court cases in which fishermen ought to have paid charges, and they have not, and their neighbours a few villages away have paid. This has caused us considerable concern.
I agree with him that this should cause concern. Ele goes on to say:
The amount of money that we are anticipating collecting in the first year, should we introduce this new scheme of charging everyone, would be extremely modest and, in fact, would only equal what we are collecting today.
That was an assurance in committee that the total amount of fees taken from commercial fishermen will not be any higher.
Let us go into the rest of the evidence. We come now to the minister's statement on January 31, 1978 made in the House when he said the following about the fees to be charged to fishermen. It is to be found at page 2414 of Hansard of that day. He said:
However, let me assure the House that no decision has been made in respect of the details of a new fee structure. Fishermen are not going to wake up with the passage of this legislation to find they have to pay the federal government "X" number of dollars.
He did not specify the number of dollars. Then he went on to say:
I believe we should continue with our present system, with all its shortcomings, for the present, without making any charges until the health of the fishery improves and subsidies in that area are reduced. What we intend to do now is discuss with fishermen and their organizations how we can achieve a modest and equitable fee structure that would allow both better management of facilities and better on-site services for Canada's commercial fishermen. Certainly I cannot emphasize this enough.
Let us look at the evidence given by the man who actually runs the system, namely, Mr. Reid. This is what he testified in front of the committee on November 24, just before the bill came out of committee:
The level of charge will be modest and reflect regional differences; in fact, we have proposed that it should range from a low of $1 per foot per year in the Atlantic regions and Quebec to $2 per foot per year in the Pacific.
That evidence indicates a 63 per cent increase in the present moorage charges in the province of British Columbia, which is the evidence I have, and the minister can re-examine that. It indicates a tremendous discrimination between one coast and the other. I am not suggesting that there should not be some discrimination in favour of those who are least able to pay, but the myth that the commercial fishermen of British Columbia are wealthy entrepreneurs just does not bear close examination. In fact, there is a great number of fishermen in British Columbia for whom the moorage fees are key to their operation and to whether they can make a satisfactory living. We are talking of up to $2,000 a year for licence fees in B.C. When you keep adding all these drips and dabs in B.C., where does that leave us? That kind of discrimination is completely unsatisfactory and unnecessary, and if we pass this bill we give a blank cheque to the minister to impose whatever fee he wants with regard to commercial fisheries.
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
I do not think this minister has done a bad job. I do not want to carp and criticize everything, but if I was a commercial fisherman, I would not buy a pig in a poke. If I was a commercial fisherman, I would want a commitment, before the minister was given the powers contained in this bill, as to what his charges will be and how many wharfingers will be hired in the province of B.C. Are these wharfingers to be local Liberals who happen to be unemployed? That question always comes up. One of the minister's principal problems might be to find Liberals to handle these jobs. Things are getting pretty rough. We do not know how many wharfingers the minister intends to add to the rolls. Some wharfingers in British Columbia work eight hours and then nip down to pick up fees at the docks. Those people are called wharfingers, but if that is the kind of wharfinger we are going to add to the ones we already have, the government can forget about it. We do not need part-time wharfingers and moonlighters. If we are going to have wharfingers, fishermen want people who will properly manage docks so they will get something for their money.
Another myth abroad is that fishermen are mooring for nothing all over the place, and they are not. It depends, but at the docks where they are allegedly mooring for nothing a fisherman would not want to tie up his boat because it might be cut adrift the next day, boats might have to get over sand bars to get to the docks, no dredging is done, the docks are rotting right into the ocean, and there is no breakwater at all.
I do not object to the idea that we should spend more money on small harbours. The minister has not spent enough money on small harbours. We can be putting public money into those harbours, but I do not see why commercial fishermen have to bear the burden. I do not see why we should take one section of the economy and let it carry the can for something this government has allowed to decline over the last 20 or 30 years.
Another reason this bill should not be approved is that there has been a remarkable lack of consultation with those involved. I know the minister has been out to the coast. I know he has had meetings with the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union. However, as I recall, the minister did not have those meetings prior to this bill going through committee. The fishermen's union was not invited to make representations to the committee with regard to this bill. That particular union, which is the most seriously affected, submitted a very lengthy and detailed brief on this subject to the minister, and my information is that that brief has not been responded to in any detailed way. The minister did spend some two and a half hours, but he did not spend two and a half hours with the representatives of that union on the question of moorage fees. He spent his time on salmon enhancement problems, with boundary problems and with U.S.-Canada treaty problems-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: And Bill C-2.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
-but how much time was spent on Bill C-2? Very little out of that two and a half hour meeting. Perhaps that is consultation in the way this government operates, but it is not meaningful consultation. Surely those who are most seriously affected by the fees should have the principal input in

February 1, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
terms of how the program is going to work and which docks are going to become staffed docks at which there will be charges.
It is perhaps typical of this government that it moves first and asks questions of the groups most affected later, but it is wrong. Having this bill in his hand will improve the minister's bargaining position with regard to fees charged to fishermen on the west coast, but I am not particularly interested in strengthening the minister's hand. The people who need help are the fishermen, not the minister. Therefore, what we should be doing is denying the minister this bill and letting him go back to the coast to meet with Pacific trawlers, the UFAWU, the native brotherhood and all the fishing groups to develop a consensus for a bill which the people affected can accept.
That is not what the minister has done. He is going to give them a bill. If they do not like it, he will listen to them for ten minutes, but they are going to get it anyway. The minister is going to ram it down the throats of British Columbia fishermen, and this being so I suggest that there will be a real problem. Some fishermen may not obey the law, and I would regret that, but the kind of approach one takes to legislation has to be considered with care. It is important to get a consensus of the commercial fishing industry of B.C. That consensus is important if there is to be no problem collecting moorage charges.
With regard to clause 8, the question of the minister's capacity to transfer public property to the private sector, I am concerned about the minister's lack of capacity to guarantee fishermen that the rates set by regulation will be maintained by the private sector and the failure to guarantee that services to vessels will be properly maintained. That is a fundamental flaw. The number of mooring stations for commercial fishermen will be reduced because the private sector wants to handle big yachts from Seattle and get the people with the bucks to pay more and more moorage fees. This is a beautiful opportunity for the minister to abandon his reponsibility to commercial Fishermen on the coast.
There are many problems in the fishing industry. The minister has not resolved the uncertainty of the A and B licensing system, and in my discussions with fishermen I learned that that is causing very real concern on the coast. The minister has not made an announcement with regard to the phase-out. I think he is putting the cart before the horse again. Fishermen want to know where they are going with regard to their licensing system.
The small harbours matter is something which could have been left alone. Fishermen would like to know whether Canada will have any clout with regard to setting boundaries. Indications are that we have given up on the Dixon entrance and on the boundary in the riding of the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) which was set by international treaty. Indications are that we are bungling on the salmon negotiations. We are not standing up. The minister cannot expect to earn the confidence of the fishing industry when Canada is rolled over by the Americans on these negotiations. The minister's department says it is doing a great job. It
[Mr. Leggatt.j
tells fishermen to forget about those negotiations and that it will increase moorage fees this year. The department says it is going to put the matter of small harbours on a sound foundation. How can fishermen have confidence in this kind of legislation when nothing has been done about other matters?
With regard to the transfer of public property to private enterprise, if the minister would limit that provision to municipal or provincial authority and limit the capacity of that authority to set moorage rates beyond those set by regulation under the legislation, then I think he would have the support of fishermen. Unless I have misread the bill, control of power to regulate fees under the terms of the lease arrangement would be lost. From a practical point of view the bill would be useless because no private marina would be interested in obtaining a public small harbour unless it had flexibility in regard to fees. Those people are in business to make a profit and are not going to hold on to the property under lease if they are losing money.
There are a lot of areas in this country other than commercial fishermen that can be taxed. If more money is needed for small harbours it is available from many areas that have been undertaxed in the past, such as the western empire which derives as much benefit from the fishing industry as any other class in Canada. Tax concessions are granted at the top level and that is where additional money could be obtained.
If we increase the number of wharfingers there is no guarantee that they will be full time wharfingers, no guarantee of their training, of what kind of people will be hired to do the job or whether the last canvasser of the Liberal party just walks down to the end of the dock and takes his position in the little hut. Most of all, there is a lack of consultation with the groups affected.
All these things lead me to the firm conclusion that this bill is premature, Mr. Speaker, and that the government should withdraw it. The minister should take another trip to the west coast and instead of just spending two and a half hours talking on the subject of moorage payments he should spend a day with the fishermen, go up to Skeena for a day or out to the Island for a day, and then come back to this bill. I cannot accept the evidence given in committee to the effect that fishermen are crying for this legislation because that just is not true, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I heard the minister's remarks at the opening of the debate I thought that I would not speak. I have a fair degree of confidence in him and respect for his ability, sincerity and integrity relative to other cabinet ministers in this government. Of course, that qualifies my commendation somewhat. I felt that the minister had addressed the problems that I raised in committee but upon reading Hansard today I found a number of qualifications that led me to believe he was perhaps using a delaying tactic. Perhaps he hoped I could be convinced to keep quiet and that the fees could be slipped into place and the bill passed. That is what my concern centres upon.

I am well aware, as are west coast fishermen, that the governor in council sets the fees under this bill and that the proclamation in the Gazette is not to be made just yet. My concern is that there should be some indication of the nature of the fees prior to passage of the bill. I expressed that concern in committee and as a result the minister presented samples of the fees that were anticipated and defended them. He stated clearly that he wants a different fee schedule for each region. The figures shown to the committee indicated that west coast fishermen will pay twice as much as their east coast counterparts. I can tell the minister that they do not like that.
The minister admits that for years inequity has been perpetrated by the Liberal government, that the administration has been inadequate and management of our harbours poor. This is the minister's own condemnation of previous ministers and this government's efforts in the fisheries industry. We are glad the government took note of our demand for change and brought this type of bill forward. We are pleased to hear they are concerned about inadequate administration and management and the history of inequalities which they claim will disappear.
The minister speaks of erasing inequalities and then goes on to say he will recognize regional differences. I should like him to recognize regional differences in the sense that the problems of the fisheries of British Columbia are not necessarily the same as those on the east coast but must be treated differently. That does not mean they should be treated differently on the basis of fee schedules or ability to pay but, rather, that the fee structure should be based on the cost of services provided. The sample presented by the minister indicated that this factor will not be taken into account.
We already have equalization in our federal system. The income tax system is supposed to redistribute income in an equitable manner. There is also the system of equilization payments between provinces which is supposed to equalize the level of services between regions. These two federal concerns at least have some clear cut direction in theory if not in practice. Then we have a whole host of federal policy initiatives with scattered effects which dot each department.
The sum total of all these initiatives to develop equalization is actually a terrible mess and the proposed fee schedule is just one more feature. We have tariffs, transportation rates, DREE programs, the Canada Works program and so on. I am concerned that this should not be just another method of redistributing income. There are other provisions and other bills to this effect. If we want to redistribute income we should use the existing programs of income tax and equalization and not carry the burden forward. We should recognize that some fishermen in British Columbia are competent and successful but that not all fishermen in British Columbia can be classed in the same way. There are poor fishermen in British Columbia just as there are in the Atlantic provinces. In fact, to be a poor fisherman in British Columbia is more a severe plight than to be a poor fisherman in the Atlantic region because the costs are so much higher, the competition is so much keener and tougher, in that province.
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
Let me make this point very strongly. I want the minister to stand up and tell us that the fee schedule will not be based on ability to pay but will be charged equally to all fishermen in British Columbia; that instead it will be a fee that relates to the cost of service and the quality of service that is provided to those fishermen.
The new berthing charges do not grasp the user-pay concept, as well they should not. Motorists do not pay for the total cost of highways directly, nor do airline patrons have to shell out for the whole cost of airports. Fishermen should not be the exception to the rule and should not be expected to pay for the full cost of servicing their industry. The berthing charges will be directed to the salaries of harbour managers. There is little reason why these people would be paid twice as much in British Columbia on the west coast as they are on the east coast, so why should the charges as indicated in the fee schedule be twice as much in British Columbia? If a fee must be charged it must be a consistent fee between the regions. The differences should be recognized in the nature of the fisheries, but not in the nature of the fee schedule.
The minister has made much of his willingness to meet with the fishermen on their own turf. He has visited the area and he has directed his officials to become acquainted with the fishermen. I appreciate the initiatives of the minister. I know these reports are true. I have received a very good response from officials in his department. They are endeavouring to be open and are prepared to bring information forward. 1 commend him for that. But yet while we see this openness, it just has not quite worked as far as consultation goes.
I have made assumptions and I took it for granted that when this bill came to committee the fishermen would in fact be invited to give testimony. In committee I questioned this very carefully. I asked if this fee schedule had been accepted by the fishermen in British Columbia and if they had been consulted. It is on record in Hansard. I was assured by the witnesses testifying, by the minister and I believe by one of the Liberal backbenchers, that in fact such consultation had taken place. I could not believe that the British Columbia fishermen would agree to pay a fee schedule twice as much as the east coast fishermen. But I was given that assurance.
I took those assurances and the minutes and I sent them to British Columbia to the fishermen's union. What do you know? The fishermen wrote back. Referring to C-2, Jack Nichol, president of the United Fishermen's and Allied Workers' Union, in a December 5 letter to the minister, stated:
At no time was our union contacted or consulted on this matter.
The union was referring to the matter of fees. So that consultation had not in fact taken place. The promise that the minister gives me today is now somewhat in doubt. Once the minister, someone in his department, or one of his officials have misled us about this consultation, we become doubtful and sceptical. And, Mr. Speaker, you can hardly blame us for that in this instance.

While I have a reasonable amount of faith in him as the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, I am rather concerned that he might in fact leave this chamber. If that were to be so, I would be very concerned about giving these broad powers to another minister who might not exercise them with the discretion that this minister appears willing to exercise.
With respect to this fee schedule, we may have to look at it again. It should be put in an amended form before we pass it. It should be considered further and perhaps even a section taken out of the bill for more study. Maybe a commitment could be made to us that the fee schedule will be attached by amendment to the bill in the next session of the House- something along this line to assure that the fishermen and all those who are directly affected can appear and make their points known to us prior to the passing of this bill. Rather than giving full discretion to the minister, perhaps there should be some limitation imposed.
I am concerned that this after-the-fact consultation is a feature, not only of this particular minister, but of government departments. In all forms of environmental legislation we constantly have the attitude: "Yes, we are concerned, but let us build the plant now and see about it later". The one exception has been the Fisheries Act. Again, I am a little concerned about this act because it is masquerading a little bit. I wish that the minister would put a little more emphasis on the fact that this is a major environmental bill, that the powers the minister has taken unto himself are in fact the only veto powers to any development available in any bill before this House respecting before-the-fact legislation.
This bill has great environmental potential. It also has a great capacity for abuse. To give an example, if I were to touch my toe in the water, I could be considered a pollutant and the development would stop. That is not a confession relative to the cleanliness of my feet!
I suggest to the minister that he consider interfacing this bill with another bill relating to the environmental impact assessment or assure us whether or not it is an environmental bill. Will it in fact be used in that capacity in lieu of other legislation? These are questions which remain unanswered and are of concern to the fishermen on the west coast.
I am pleased to see that my representations which I have made continually since I have been here as a member of the House of Commons regarding recreational boating promotion have resulted from the fact that British Columbia has a tremendous coastline but has virtually no facilities for small boats. Small boats are constantly being forced to travel to the United States in order to gain berthing in Bellingham and Blaine. There is a great demand and need for recreational boating and for harbours in British Columbia. I am pleased to see that the minister has recognized this need after much pushing from myself and others. An hon. member seems to question when I have done this. If the hon. member will look at the first speech which I gave in the House of Commons, he will find it there. If he would review the committee meetings for the fisheries department he will find it there too. In addition to that, if the minister would like to consult my constituents who
[Mr. Wenman.J
have worked with the minister to assist in bringing information forward, he will find it again, and again.
I have one small doubt here concerning the improvement, expansion and the updating of wharves. With respect to the wharf at Ruskin, where the local council and the local fishermen need the wharf, I received notice two months ago that they are tearing it down. This matter does not seem to jell when we are talking of maintaining, rebuilding and expanding. At the same time I am trying to tell the people of the area that the Minister is saying the wharf must be torn down. This is just an example of policy which needs to be referred to the minister's department to check. Are they operating under the auspices of this bill or are they still operating on the theory of efficiency with a lot of cutting back over the past few years?
With those points in mind I would like to say that I approve of the principle of this bill, the consolidation of it and the fact that the minister will be able to make decisions and actually do something concrete under the provisions thereof. Those are the positive aspects and the reason why the bill should pass.
But there are weaknesses. There is great concern for Canadian unity in this country and the recognition of the differences of the regions. But for goodness sake we must not play one coast against the other coast. Equity must be found, and I am sure it will be found if there is further and better consultation on the fee structure and the other items which are concerning our fishermen.

I would be more than pleased to entertain a question at the close of my remarks.
To move on to the criticisms concerning the abandonment and destruction of facilities, let me remind hon. members opposite that the department has not abandoned any usable and useful small craft harbour facilities. I would say that some facilities have been abandoned as no longer being used. These are few in number and account for less than one per cent of the facilities.
In total, facilities have increased. However, it is obvious it makes no economic sense to spend money on facilities which
Fishing and Recreational Harbours are no longer required while leaving harbours used by fishermen to go begging. The government's approach is a rational one-to improve facilities where required and to abandon those no longer serving any useful purpose. As a result of consultation with municipalities and members of this House, facilities which are borderline have often been improved over the last few years through the Canada Works and similar government programs, using local labour, thereby providing a double spin-off in terms of employment and usable facilities for which departmental priorities would not normally dictate the expenditure of funds.
On the recreational side, although limited funds are expended these do contribute to the public's access to the water, as well as providing economic benefit in terms of employment. I should make it clear that federal funds allocated to community marina developments contain guarantees that such facilities are always open and available to the public. This program recognizes the importance of recreational boating and the rapidly expanding demand for public berthing. Of course, the government is not in a position to develop and operate totally recreational facilities. Our position is one of assistance in areas of greatest need.
Turning to the matter of consultation with the provinces, I can assure hon. members opposite that consultation did take place with regard to this bill on many occasions. As recently as the summer of 1977, the provinces were again asked for their views. Apparently some members have forgotten the committee discussions covering this point. We are not surprised by criticism emanating from certain newspapers in different parts of Canada, but surely members of the committee were apprised of the situation and correspondence was produced during the committee hearings.
I wish to comment on the matter of fees. I notice that the hon. member who spoke immediately before me is no longer here. There is good reason for the fact that in the bill itself no schedule of fees is set down. During the committee hearings the former director of small craft harbours explained that no fee system can be "cast in concrete", and the fact that no fee schedule is attached to the legislation allows the minister to discuss fees with British Columbia, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia before they are imposed. Consultation can take place as to the fees which should properly be charged.
I believe that everyone on the standing committee was aware there is no fee schedule included in Bill C-2. Certainly the minister has indicated on numerous occasions that the fee schedule will not be the subject of capricious decision by either himself or his officials. Rather, it will be the result of a process of deliberation, a process of meeting with those concerned in order to make sure a fair determination is reached in setting it up.
It is not as though there is no fee system already in effect. We have fee systems on both the east and west coasts. Certain members who have spoken in this debate indicated to the House, I am sure not deliberately, that there is some new concept, that the government of Canada, under the present Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), has
80031 -14'/2

February 1, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours suddenly backed away from the system of charging fees to those who use commercial fishing facilities. This is far from the truth, Mr. Speaker. We have had a system in place on the west coast for a number of years. The problem is that fishermen dependent on the wharves and harbours they use are being discriminated against. Fishermen may pay a fee in one port but not in another. Fishermen get together and discuss what is going on in the industry. It would be no surprise if one fishermen asked: "What the devil is going on? I am being charged fees when you are not."
Surely the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leg-gatt) will agree that if you use a facility, there should be some charge to the user. I think the hon. member will also agree that the fee should be determined after consultation with those who are going to use the facility. The bill does not include a fee schedule.
The hon. member can say the minister is going to bring in a fee that will be totally unreasonable for fishermen in the province of British Columbia. I suspect from the past performance of this minister that the opposite is the case. Fishermen on both the east and west coasts of Canada have come to trust this minister because what he says he usually does.
The minister recently returned from a week's visit to British Columbia. I think his consultation is an indication that he is willing to listen to the UFAWU, the trawlers, processors, native groups and others in British Columbia. That is the process that will have to go on regarding fees and the establishment of berthage charges is concerned.
As I have said, I am pleased to support this legislation. It is rational. It has been on the books for two or three years awaiting third reading. I am surprised that some opponents of the legislation have suggested that we are rushing into it. If a span of two or three years is rushing into a situation, I would hate to see what would happen if we actually passed legislation within a month. It is funny, but people in Canada say one of two things. If they are in favour of a piece of legislation, they say we should get it through and quit dragging our feet. If we rush to deal with it, we are accused of ramrodding it through.
If a piece of legislation has been before this House for two or three years, I do not accept the statement that those in the fishing industry have not had an opportunity to make their views known. I suggest that anyone interested in this legislation has had ample opportunity to come before this House and make any representations that they wish.
The hon. member who spoke before me said that invitations were not sent out. Surely it is not the role of parliament to send out invitations asking every Canadian if he wishes to appear before a standing committee. Most fishing industry representatives keep a very close watch on what is happening in the House of Commons with regard to legislation that affects their industry. I suspect the reason why there was not a great deal of representation to the committee was that, by and large, the industry was in favour of it. I do not think the fact that one or two groups have expressed the desire to halt the

legislation at this point will find total agreement across Canada, from one coast to the other.
For this reason, I am very pleased to support this legislation and congratulate the minister for having brought it before the House.

Mr. Speaker, I want to use this occasion to bring to the attention of the minister some problems peculiar to the fishermen of Glace Bay in my constituency. I want to deal with the concept of management and control that was introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). This was referred to in another way by the last speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson). The second concept I want to speak on in relation to this bill and the problem in my area is the question of consultation.
Very recently the question of a slipway and repair shed for Glace Bay harbour was finally solved. Agreement has been reached with the small craft harbours branch, which got Treasury Board to move on this federal labour intensive project and received their money from them.
When the order was put in for the material required for the slipway, they ordered treated lumber. Untreated lumber was received and it cannot be used, and the fishermen are rather worked up about this. They were kept waiting many months for the slipway; Treasury Board was very slow in giving approval. Now that Treasury Board has finally approved the FLIP money, the material to build the slipway must be sent back because it is untreated.
The fishermen are very concerned about the question of management and control. They have already brought this to the attention of the small craft harbour officials. I understood the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to say that through this bill there is the possibility of putting controls on piers, harbours and so on, under such groups as fishermen's associations, co-operatives-

That is a question I am asking. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni seemed to suggest that. What we in Glace Bay want is control of that skidway under the fishermen's association, something similar to what the co-op has in Cheticamp. It is true they have a marine railway.

I can swear to you, Mr. Minister, that one fisherman in Glace Bay paid $8,500 to use that private marine railway in Sydney.
Given the income situation of inshore fishermen on the whole of the east coast, particularly in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, this is inequitable. The only way to correct it is to allow the fishermen to manage that slipway and repair shed

once it is completed. There will have to be a fee structure for use, and agreement from those who do not belong to the fishermen's association.
On my last journey back to my constituency some two weeks ago, I met with the fishermen. They informed me that the money being used to build that slipway and repair shed would be wasted unless they could control and manage it; otherwise, it would end up in a shambles. I am inclined to agree with them. 1 would ask the minister if he would consider this and get an expression in writing to this fishermen's association through the head of the small craft and harbours branch. This has little to do with management and moorage fees, because in my particular part of the world this question has not been brought to my attention as being a major problem. One thing that is very clear when you come into this House at first is the significant differences between west coast and east coast fishing.
I take exception to what was said by one member speaking for the Conservative side today. He expressed the opinion, as I understood him, and I hope I am not misinterpreting him, that west coast fishermen, or a lot of them, are much worse off than Atlantic Fishermen. If it were not for unemployment insurance and other things they receive they would be in even worse shape.
I say these things knowing, as those of us who are in any way connected with fisheries know, that this minister has done his best in the short period of time he has been in office to make up for the failures of this government vis-a-vis the inshore fishermen which have taken place for at least 15 years. That minister will admit, in all humility, that there is still a very, very long way to go.

As far as consultation is concerned, I know the minister recently spent a week in British Columbia consulting the people there, but that is a very large area. He also spent a considerable amount of time in the Atlantic region in those areas more heavily dependent upon the Fishing industry than is my region. As most members know, even if they go to sleep when I get to my feet, most of my riding is made up of miners, with about 25 per cent of the work force employed by the Sydney steel plant in my riding and a smaller percentage of fishermen and loggers. Let us compare Cape Breton on the east coast with the metropolitan area of Halifax in respect of what has happened with the inshore fisheries. It seems obvious that the people in the department, particularly in the small craft harbours branch, were convinced that fisheries should be written off in the area as far as potential is concerned. I have talked about this matter with Devco as well, particularly regarding inshore fishing. It is one thing to let inshore fishing gradually die out in an area within a 50 or 60 miles radius from Halifax because Halifax has mushroomed in growth. There is also a special problem there now regarding ship repairing by Hawker Siddeley. But that is another concern. I suggest that anything Hawker Siddeley has touched in the maritime provinces has ultimately turned to lead anyway. That company has continually been propped up through subsidies, and so on. The government has given them substantial subsidies in Cape Breton, yet the company walked off and left us high and dry. The government then had to take up what cudgels there were left, along with the social problems and so on. I do not think it did a good job in that regard, although I appreciate the enormous effort it has recently made in respect of the coal industry. However, most of the time the government is darn reluctant to accept the notion that you have to make some kind of plans, especially in regions where there are only one or two other industries. Planning before hand is replaced by reactive planning.
Let me return to this notion of comparing the area around Sydney with that of metropolitan Halifax. Sydney is essentially the large population area of Cape Breton. I am speaking of the region close to Sydney, Glace Bay, Donkin and other such areas where the fishing industry has died or is dying. Because in addition to the seasonally unemployed in Fishing there is average unemployment of 20 per cent to 25 per cent in the other sectors. Because of the growth in the metropolitan Halifax area and what has been done there for Halifax and Dartmouth through DREE and other programs, you can disregard the people who have been involved in inshore fishing for a long period of time. However, to do that in eastern Nova Scotia would create absolute catastrophe, because all you are doing is perpetuating a bad situation, and some government or combination of governments will eventually have to spend a lot

It is terribly important to the fishermen in the area to have management and control of such things as slipways in their areas, although they have been considered as not having as much potential in the inshore fisheries as perhaps in other areas of Nova Scotia. Obviously they have pretty nearly been dependent exclusively on the fishing industry, and when they are offered such things by the government in the way of help to the fishing industry they feel such assistance should be put under their control and management, although they agree that regulations and rules must be established and approved of by the Department of Fisheries. In addition to the management and consultation questions- and I am repeating myself now and probably rambling a bit- the minister has been down into my area for the purpose of consultation. He came down at the request of the Sydney industrial board of trade. The unfortunate thing is that while the sponsors were well-intentioned, they do not know the fishermen very well. The department was also well intentioned, but the result was that the minister received only a small representation from the fishing areas.
These fishermen want the minister to come back to that area. They have a lot of questions to ask him. Inshore fishermen have a great deal of respect for this minister as compared to the minister whose place he took. This minister has taken an unequivocal stand in respect of inshore fishermen as opposed to offshore fishing which we know is also important. They want him back to explain the philosophy he expounded in Yarmouth. They want him to explain how this philosophy is to be turned into policy in respect of inshore fishing. They are convinced now that the minister is for them, but they also know there is a strong group in the Nova Scotia government area that wants to place most of the emphasis and spend most of the money on offshore fisheries, with very little emphasis being placed on the inshore fisheries.
Mr. Alphonse Bergeron, who is the son of a fisherman in my area, lives at 3 Park Street, Sydney, Nova Scotia. He reminded me that the "Fishing News International" of October 1977 reported that according to Dr. Dan Reid, who is the minister of fisheries for Nova Scotia, his department wanted $135 million to be spent on nine freezer trawlers; $600 million to be spent on 125 new trawlers; and $140 million to be spent to replace old scallop draggers. I am sure it is possible for the minister to meet with 100 to 150 fishermen in the eastern Nova Scotia area whom we could attract in order to discuss these and other problems which they face. I appeal to Mr. Hall, who is in the gallery, and I hope the minister will take note of what I am saying.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make with respect to the bill before the House. I welcome the opportunity it affords those of us who come from provinces and constituencies where the fishing industry is an important factor. It provides us with an opportunity to have some input into the fisheries policy in an attempt to improve legislation. Of course, that is the raison d'etre behind this kind of parliamentary debate.
Notwithstanding the fact that this bill has been around for some considerable time, I must say I read the minister's speech which he presented in the House last night very carefully and could find nothing in it to reassure me there would be no additional financial burden imposed upon Canadian fishermen at this time. As reported at page 2414 of Hansard, the minister said the following:
However, let me assure the House that no decision has been made in respect of the details of a new fee structure. Fishermen are not going to wake up with the passage of this legislation to find they have to pay the federal government "X" number of dollars.
As the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) said so eloquently, we may wake up to find that the hon. member opposite is no longer with us and has gone on to what he considers to be greener pastures. Consequently, that assurance is no longer valid. As long as the minister is in his post, he can be held to his word. With the transpiration of events, there is every indication he will accept the siren call from New Brunswick and leave us for the Liberal leadership of that province.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
I wish him godspeed and every happiness. I cannot wish him success because I know he cannot achieve that, even if I wish it. I believe the minister is leaving, which makes it incumbent upon us to do what we can to get him to change his mind on this bill. That is why the hon. member for
February 1, 1978

South Shore indicated that our party cannot support this bill at this time.
The bill provides us with an excellent opportunity to speak on fisheries and fishery policy generally. I regret very much the minister did not seize this opportunity in his speech last night, because a lot of fish have been caught and a lot of water has flowed in the northwest Atlantic and Pacific since the introduction of this bill. Many important changes are taking place in this industry, the oldest of Canada's industries. They are welcome changes brought about as a result of the unilateral declaration and imposition of the 200-mile economic zone, which was preceded by various bilateral agreements with a number of countries that have enjoyed ancient, traditional fishing rights in some of the areas now covered by that zone.
It has been indicated that it will take anywhere from five years to ten years to build up the stocks in order to repair the damage which was done as a result of the uncontrolled foreign exploitation that took place in our fishing grounds. It will be necessary to take advantage of that period of time in order to put in place policies which will have long term effects and which will provide Canadians with a certain degree of confidence that has heretofore been missing in this industry. It should be the kind of confidence men and women can build their futures upon and be reasonably assured of a good living. The Atlantic Canada fishing industry has a potential of providing our people with a good way of living and with a good income. Certainly this holds true in the case of Newfoundland, which is currently experiencing economic difficulties that are prevalent across the country. When there is an economic crisis in Canada, it becomes all that much more severe in Atlantic Canada which already faces the highest unemployment rate in our country.
A number of our people who no longer have any confidence in fly-by-night industrial ventures-and rightly so when you look at the record of some of these ventures-are now beginning to look to the fishing industry because they believe that there is a future in the fishery. They know that with our management of the stock we can now control the industry to the point where we can maximize the exploitation of it for the benefit of our own people, which has not been the case heretofore.
In the past, it is true to say, the fishing industry has been a Cinderella of the Canadian government. We have had a number of ministers who preceded the hon. gentleman who now has the responsibility of the fisheries portfolio, earnest, sincere, dedicated people, whose influence on their colleagues in cabinet, unfortunately for the fishing industry, has been minimal. Consequently, matters relating to the fisheries were always given a very low priority. But now I hope that is changing, and I suspect a symptom of that change in attitude by the House is the attention that has been paid to this bill.
In normal times a bill of this nature brought before the House would only receive perfunctory attention. It would be passed through all phases of the parliamentary process quite
Fishing and Recreational Harbours quickly. But not so today because we all sense there is something happening. In fact, we know there is something happening. We know there are big things in store, and therefore this debate provides us with the first opportunity we have to discuss matters relating to the fishery.
As far as the industry in Newfoundland is concerned, I have stated-and I firmly believe, and the government of Newfoundland believes-that the fishing industry has the potential to provide our people with a good livelihood, to provide excellent job and business opportunities for our people, if we go about it the right way. But regrettably, all is not as it should be. What I call a jurisdictional debate has developed between the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) and his counterpart in the government of Newfoundland, to the detriment of the industry. I want to be as objective as I can. The gentleman who holds the responsibility for the fisheries portfolio in Newfoundland is a former member of the House and I believe-and I feel in all fairness that the minister opposite will agree with me-that he is certainly one of the best fisheries ministers that Newfoundland has ever had, if not the best. He has brought to the portfolio a dedication and a concern that has all too often been missing in the past.
Out of that concern and dedication, in consultation with his counterpart in the province of Nova Scotia-because essentially when we speak of the groundfish industry in the Atlantic provinces we are primarily talking about Newfoundland and Nova Scotia-he has put together a fisheries development program. The minister complained that he has not even seen the program, that the program had never been presented to him. I find that hard to believe because I suspect, indeed 1 know, that the minister's officials had a great deal of input in the preparation of that program. Civil servants in the provincial and federal jurisdictions in this field of activity have worked and continue to work very closely together, and rightly so. The minister knew what was in the program, but he seemed to want to go his own separate way.
What we on this side of the House would like to see implemented is the philosophy expounded by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson), who issued a major statement on fisheries on January 26 in the form of a press release and an excellent paper, with most of which I find myself in total agreement. He said:
It is important, even essential, that fishermen, the fish trade, governments and Newfoundlanders generally, work together co-operatively to make the most of this new chance because, the odds are, that if we fail this time, that chance won't come again.
I say Amen to that statement. I believe that the situation is improving. 1 believe that there is emerging from the dispute to which I have referred a new climate of co-operation. I give a lot of the credit for this to the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who represents one of the important fishing constituencies in this country. He initiated, with the support of his colleague the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), a symposium on the fisheries at Marystown, and from that I think has emerged a new spirit of co-operation.

February 1, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
I believe there will now be very close co-operation by the two levels of government, certainly in so far as the fisheries development is concerned in the province of Newfoundland, because there are problems that have to be tackled. One of them is the whole question of the utilization of the resource. At present it is underutilized. Both our present plant capacity and our trawler capacity are underutilized, and that is a situation which we must turn around.
Then there is the question-I am sure this is a question which is very dear to the minister's heart, and I do not say that sarcastically because I know it is and I applaud him for it-of inshore fisheries. Up to the extension of our jurisdiction, the inshore fishery had a very limited future because the fish were not coming in. They were not coming in because they were being caught by foreigners. It is as simple as that. Now we have a chance to control that situation, and an opportunity to develop a viable inshore industry so that a man can engage in the fishing industry with very little investment in terms of facilities, and so on, if he utilizes smaller boats and if he has some kind of assurance that there will be proper holding facilities for his catch until the plants are able to absorb it. In that lies the greatest opportunity for expansion, and not only for expansion but for the preservation of what the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the president of the Newfoundland Fish Food and Allied Workers' Union has called Newfoundland's social structure. It is an opportunity for the preservation of a way of life that has existed in our province for over 400 years, the very reason for the existence of Newfoundland in the first place.
I hope that we can provide these fishermen with incentives and not put road blocks in their way. I consider this bill to be a potential road block. It is another part of the user-pay concept of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). We are liable to wake up tomorrow and find the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has become the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition in the province of New Brunswick, and lo and behold there it is!

speechtext:
I believe we should be, at this critical stage in our fisheries development, providing incentives to our people to involve themselves in the inshore fishery. Here I want to refer-and I regret very much having to bring this partisan note in here-to the minister's pork barrel philosophy in approaching the whole business of allocation of funds to small craft harbours. I can cite my constituency as living proof that this pork barrel approach to the allocation of funds for wharves, breakwaters and marine facilities still exists and in fact is thriving under the administration of the present minister. Notwithstanding its urban nature, my constituency, as the minister knows, is a very important fish producing constituency. There are a number of small harbours adjacent to the city of St. John's which are the headquarters for a number of inshore and mid-shore fishermen. Yet try as we may, we are unable to get the government to give any priority to repairs and construction of new facilities in the constituency of St.
[Mr. McGrath.)
John's East. I suspect the same probably holds true in the riding of St. John's West.
Just let me give an example by way of illustration. Between Christmas and New Year's we had an unusual storm. Even the oldtimers could not remember anything to come close to it in terms of ferocity and severity. We suspect there was some kind of subterranean upheaval. It almost caused a tidal wave. It was devastating and did a tremendous amount of damage in the southeast part of Newfoundland.
I met with fishermen from several important fishing communities in my constituency where damage had been extensive, and together with the fishermen's union, the mayor, provincial officials and officials from the minister's department we came to the conclusion that there was a serious problem. In order to ensure that it would be addressed expeditiously and urgently we sent a telex to the minister outlining the extent of the damage, requesting immediate attention to it and calling upon the minister to get on with the business of providing additional facilities. In this case we wanted breakwaters to ensure that this kind of storm damage would never recur; in other words, to ensure that we would not be spending good money after bad.
I must say that the minister's response was sympathetic. I talked to his officials, and I received a letter from the minister concerning the villages of Torbay and Flat Rock. It is here that we get into the pork barrel philosophy of the minister. As a courtesy to me as a member of parliament surely the minister could have given me the opportunity of telling these people that the damage would be repaired and that the Department of Public Works had been instructed to investigate the possibility of putting in breakwaters. But no, letters arrived three days after the minister's announcement appeared in the St. John's press. That is a discourtesy.
We have come to expect that because the minister exemplifies and epitomizes the pork barrel approach, and I say that is regrettable. The industry is too important and too critical for us to resurrect that ancient and outmoded approach to the building of marine works and the repairing of existing facilities. The fishermen in my constituency have just as much right to expect favourable consideration as the fishermen in a constituency represented by a Liberal, and that has not always been the case.
Let us examine the votes for small craft harbours. In 1973-74 the total was $2.9 million for the province of Newfoundland. Last night the minister referred to the 2,000 harbours and wharves which are under his jurisdiction, many of them in dire need of repair when he took them over in 1973. Most of these harbours, wharves and breakwaters are in the province of Newfoundland because of the extent of our coastline, and yet in 1973-74 the total vote was $2.9 million for Newfoundland.
The figure improved in 1974-75. It went up to $6.8 million. In 1975-76 the figure went down to $4.3 million. When we were going through a period of austerity in government spend-
February 1, 1978

ing, as pointed out by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), small craft harbours were the first to come under the knife. That is a matter of considerable regret because the small craft harbours division of the department had been underfunded for a considerable time anyway.
There was some improvement in 1976-77. The figure jumped up to $11.5 million. A very substantial portion of that, almost three quarters of it, was funds provided under the Canada Works program. That may seem logical and sensible on the surface, but in my view it represents something totally reprehensible. The minister used the Canada Works program as a means of getting cheap labour because he knew that under the program you are allowed to pay only the prevailing provincial minimum wage plus $15 which, in the case of Newfoundland, amounted to $115 per week.
An example of the problems that caused could be found at one harbour in my constituency in the town of Holyrood where there was substantial development going on, largely funded by Canada Works and with a great deal of input by the provincial government. The minister decided, and rightly so, that here was a suitable client to receive money under the marina policy of the department. It was decided that under the marina policy this project would be supported. The project was the building of a basin for a very impressive yacht club, the only one in that part of the province. It was decided to support the financing of the construction of a breakwater. So the breakwater was constructed under the marina policy. There was a contract for the hiring of workers at $6 an hour, while their neighbours employed by Canada Works who were doing the same job were getting $2.50 an hour. How totally unfair! These people could not understand what was going on, and I had to explain to them that under the regulations imposed under this program the government could pay them only the minimum wage, plus $15.
This other project came under another policy, and the contractor had to pay prevailing rates. Quite naturally, those people did not know what I was talking about, and I do not blame them, because it did not make any sense. I know of wharves throughout my constituency and throughout Newfoundland which are utilizing the cheap labour concept of Canada Works to do badly needed and long overdue repairs. That is a totally reprehensible approach to what is essentially an urgent problem. It is also the wrong way to utilize the Canada Works program, which was never intended to be utilized in that way.
I had to go along with it, and I have gone along with it. We all have because we have had no choice. If there is a wharf in a constituency which is badly in need of repairs and which the department has refused to repair because of budgetary considerations, I have to suggest an application for a grant under the Canada Works program be made, and the small craft harbours division of the Department of Fisheries supports the project and provides materials. On the surface that seems like a good idea. Canada Works supplies $100,000 for labour at $2.50 an hour where normally the labour would cost twice that amount. The Department of Fisheries supplies the materials,
Fishing and Recreational Harbours which might amount to another $20,000 or $30,000. Naturally, advantage has to be taken of this. There is no choice. It is Hobson's choice. However, I submit that this is misusing the intent of the Canada Works program, and it represents what I consider to be the frustration of the minister's officials in recognizing the need which is there but in not having the wherewithal to do anything about it. The minister does not seem to have the necessary clout with Treasury Board to get the funds to put these projects in place.
There is also the policy, which I hope will be changed, of the "chicken and egg" concept. The department will turn down a request for extension of a wharf because, on the basis of their survey, not enough fish are being landed or there is no commercial fishing activity that would justify the expenditure. How can there be when the facility is not there in the first place? Which comes first-increased fish landings or improved facilities to accommodate such landings? I hope the "chicken and egg" concept will change within the scope of the new opportunities we now have. We have a unique and golden opportunity to develop this industry as a viable and renewable one which will provide permanent jobs for as far ahead as man can see. The demand for protein will continue and will grow as the population of the world increases.
The change of attitude has to start with the minister. I know that is difficult for him, representing as he does the town of Shediac. We know the hanky-panky that went on between Shediac and Moncton. It will be difficult for the minister to change but change he must. Knowing the rules of the game as I do and having been around politics for so long, if the minister were to tell me he will spend $100,000 in my constituency, I would not make a big deal of it. People know there is a Liberal government in Ottawa, so if the minister extended that courtesy to me I would notify, as is my responsibility as their representative, the chairman of the fishermen's committee, the local of the fishermen's union, the mayor of the community concerned and the provincial member. Apparently that courtesy is not to be extended, however.
This industry is very important in Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker. I have been to Iceland and I saw how they were able to develop their industry. I can appreciate the parallel between that country and Newfoundland. The fishing industry provides them with a standard of living higher than ours-probably fourth or fifth in the world and with practically zero unemployment.
That brings me to my next comment, Mr. Speaker, the question of changes necessary to the Fisheries Act because of the 200-mile limit. The time is long past for the minister to give serious consideration to changing the Fisheries Act in order to allow foreign trawlers and draggers the right to change their crews and to have minor repairs done in Canada. The reason for the prohibition is no longer relevant. The prohibition made a great deal of sense prior to the 200-mile limit because then we had to do whatever we could to discourage foreigners from raping those resources.

February 1, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
Now we have a degree of control within 200 miles. This is another advantage which we can maximize by allowing foreigners to change crews and have minor repairs done here. This would mean a great deal to the ports of St. John's, Sydney, Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick. It would mean millions of dollars in new business and new jobs. It would mean utilizing the port of St. John's which is uniquely suited to be the service station of the North Atlantic.
The government must be sympathetic and provide proper haulout facilities. By that I mean providing a synchro-lift for the port of St. John's. We have a drydock there that is capable of expansion if we had a synchro-lift that would enable us to haul ships out of the water in order to repair their bottoms. The minister is nodding his head, Mr. Speaker. I know from what he said in the House today that active consideration is being given to this proposition. It is something that is long overdue.
Now I come to the area of foreign involvement and the question of joint ventures, Mr. Speaker. There is also the question of foreign draggers being licensed to land fish in Canada and the potential of transshipment in bond for foreigners. This has great possibilities for us. The question was taboo a short time ago but the situation has changed. There are now possibilities of working out some means of transshipment, whilst retaining control, which would provide jobs. At the moment we control the resource to a large extent. In the area outside the 200-mile limit we can exercise control through the ICNAF treaty if we go about it the right way and use the tremendous bargaining power we have as a lever. This matter was touched on by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). We could reach agreement, I am sure, for some degree of control beyond the 200-mile limit.
Of course, the 200-mile limit is just as artificial as the 12-mile limit or the three-mile limit. Had the anchovies of Peru swum for 400 miles then we would probably have a 400-mile limit. It was only because the precedent had been set by Peru to control the anchovy stock by extending their jurisdiction to 200 miles that we were able to get approval, notwithstanding the failure of the Law of the Sea Conference. We might get agreement to control beyond the 200-mile limit if we use the position of strength that we have as a bargaining lever.
We should be looking at the potential which exists not only for our ports but for our underutilized plant capacity in the Atlantic provinces, especially Newfoundland. That does not mean that we have to sell out to foreign companies. I share the minister's concern about the proposed takeover of the Ocean Harvester's plant by the subsidiary of Unilever, Nordzee. Here I Find myself on the horns of a dilemma. I see immediate jobs on the one hand and a loss of potential on the other.

I think that sums up the position this company is in, as well as other west European companies. So we can get deals without selling out. Northern stocks are crucial to the future of the inshore Fishery on the northeast and southeast coast of Newfoundland. We have already bartered away unilaterally-and I say unilaterally without reference to the government of Newfoundland-hundreds of thousands of pounds of fish through bilateral agreements. I look at the figures for 1977-178,000 metric tons of codfish with a landed value of $59 million or an export value of $118,320,000. That represents jobs that may have been lost to us by allowing foreigners to fish for these quotas. Before we make any more deals with anybody there should be first of all consultation with the province that is to be directly affected. These are our resources and they are just as important to us in Newfoundland as the oil reserves of the tar sands in Alberta are to the Albertans. It is just as much our resource. It has a tremendous impact on our economic future.
I do not think the minister, notwithstanding the constitution or any right he may feel he has constitutionally in this respect, has the right, given the concept of co-operative federalism, to barter away our future in this way without reference to us. I could go down the list of all the other species; redfish or ocean perch, 55,000 metric tons bartered away in 1977 representing $9 million or an export value of $20 million. And so it goes.
The minister laughs. The minister knows what is happening. What has been happening is that I suspect that these quotas have been used as barter in making deals with other countries for other commodities.

Yet, in terms of taxable dollars, the hon. member for Niagara Falls knows full well that his constituency gets more than its fair share.
To use the excuse that this bill has been before the House for debate for two years is spurious, and the hon. member should know better than to say so. It has not been before the House for two years. Last night the government thought that once again it might just be able to catch the opposition off guard so it tried to sneak it in. They did so. But the government has never yet caught the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) off guard, and they have never yet caught the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) off guard. Nor will they.
