speechtext:
I am thoroughly familiar with the legislation. I have sat on the committee with the hon. member for Niagara Falls and I have studied the bill from cover to cover. He clearly fails to understand that, in his representations to the minister a few moments ago, he totally neglected, in his desire to extend the marina facilities in his constituency, to indicate that there should be provincial and municipal involvement.
Let us get to the other inequities. If members opposite feel there are inequities, how do members on the opposition side feel about it? The member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Young) talked of obstructionism and delay. This bill was introduced last night. Is it obstructionism that we would seek to debate the bill for one or two days? If in the view of that member bills should be brought in and passed without debate, we have lost the true intent of parliament.
I recall other inequities with regard to the boating industry that were brought in by this government. I recall the spurious argument being introduced that, as an energy saving device, the government was going to tax certain boat motors over and above a certain size, beginning at a certain date, provided those motors were purchased from that date forward. There was no mention of the motors that were popping around the bays prior to that date. Those motors were exempt. There must have been some special designation that implied they did not consume the gasoline that the more recent motors consumed.
Fishing and Recreational Harbours What a ridiculous type of excuse that this government made on the basis of a very shallow argument.
Again to satisfy the hon. member for Niagara Falls, I am sure there are members here who agree that there is much within the content of Bill C-2 that is favourable. It is unusual to hear members on both sides of the House make statements which are clearly in favour of the minister. That rarely happens. It is a reflection of the manner in which the minister has handled his post that members from both sides of the House recognize his energies. That is not to say that improvements cannot be made. It is not to say that the minister, engrained in the Liberal tradition of confrontation with the provinces and the Liberal tradition of pork barrelling, is not a victim of those failures.
I recall after first being elected being in the small community of Procter, where there was a federal government wharf that was in a disastrous state of repair. One of the first things drawn to my attention after the election was the fact that two ladies who walked out on to this wharf in Kootenay Lake stepped on a plank and nearly ended up in the water underneath the wharf because the plank was rotten.
I was asked what I was going to do about this, and I wrote a letter to the Department of Transport. After a very substantial delay I received a response to the effect that the matter belonged more appropriately with the Department of Public Works, so I wrote a letter to the minister. Because the delay was so long, I had the opportunity to slip into a standing committee meeting involving that particular minister. I described the circumstances and asked what he was going to do about the Procter wharf.
Some weeks later I received a letter indicating that this was more appropriately the responsibility of the Department of Transport. I then wrote back to the Department of Transport, pointing out the difference of opinion and suggesting they were playing games with me and my constituents. I finally discovered the responsibility for the wharf had been taken over by small craft harbours branch of the Department of the Environment. That was in 1974.

Fishing and Recreational Harbours
1 hope this bill will provide some cohesive policy in terms of the maintenance of facilities. Looking at the wharf and ramp facilities put in by the federal government in my constituency, it seems to have been the policy to allow these facilities to deteriorate to the point where they must be declared abandoned structures, dangerous to the public and marked "Please keep off'. It would be less costly to the taxpayer to provide proper maintenance. They are all in fresh water. They are not subject to the dry rot and other erosions that occur in salt water, yet they have been allowed to deteriorate and degenerate.
There are no launching facilities on magnificent Kootenay Lake from the city of Nelson right through to the top end of the lake. Kaslo, which has its own little harbour and marina, has a private facility. The people of Kaslo and Kootenay West have been urging that the wharf be upgraded so that they can use it. The answer is: (a) the wharf has deteriorated to the stage where it is dangerous for public use; (b) too costly to repair; (c) too costly to replace; and (d) to remove the structure and put in place an earth filled structure is too costly.
We are faced with a struggle with the British Columbia government for a release of other land in that harbour to try and put in a facility for boat launching for public use on the west side of Kootenay Lake from Nelson to the head end of the lake.
Robson has the same problem. Fortunately there is a good wharf there which has been improved and is being maintained in a state of repair by the Department of the Environment. Unfortunately, there is a breakdown in communications and a failure of the two governments to get their act together. The wharf provides access to Arrow Lake below the Keenleyside dam, that structure put in under the Columbia River treaty. It is not cleared of snow in the winter. It would take a department of highways truck about ten minutes to clear that wharf. Flowever, they do not do that. As a result, no one can use it.
The same situation applies in the town of Nakusp, where the wharf has been allowed to deteriorate. When it gets into a shabby state because of the terrific rise and fall of Arrow Lake, due to the Columbia River and B.C. Hydro, the village is expected to handle the movement of that wharf facility when the water is low, to allow the dockage points to be moved out, and to have them brought in when the water is high. Finally, it looks as though B.C. Hydro is back in the act. Quite possibly with the efforts of the community of Nakusp and surrounding communities B.C. Hydro will now move and put in appropriate wharf facilities. Whether or not small craft harbours or Canada Works will join them remains to be seen. There is, however, an application that will shortly go before the minister, and that application is from the city of Nelson.
As I have already remarked, there are no boat launching facilities on Kootenay Lake for public use from Nelson to the north end of the lake, a distance of some 75 or 80 miles. There are two or three private marinas that are well maintained, but the city of Nelson has a very old marina, very old, indeed. In

its efforts to improve its foreshore Nelson now proposes to develop a marina on the foreshore site at the city of Nelson. That project will probably cost in the area of $230,000. Already the city has either approached or very shortly will approach the provincial authorities for assistance. On its behalf it would be my intention to approach small craft harbours and Canada Works. Hopefully we can see that project go ahead for the betterment of a community which exists on a lake but has no adequate or proper wharf facilities.
It should also be mentioned in the context of British Columbia, and certainly in the context of Kootenay West, that the co-operation I have received from officials of small craft harbours based in Vancouver has been very good. I should like to say I enjoy the sense of rapport which seems to have developed between myself and Mr. Warren Parkinson. His co-operation has on more than one occasion been of some benefit to the people of Kootenay West.
At the present time the provision of wharf, ramp or marina facilities is important to the boating public on that major body of water, Kootenay Lake. This is also important on the Arrow lakes, but there is less traffic there. Kootenay Lake enjoys a great deal of traffic both Canadian and American.
I might point out that recently the RCMP moved in in respect of these American boats tied up at certain marinas in my riding. These boats apparently had come through customs without proper declaration as to why they were remaining in Canada. They have been subsequently seized.
It might have been of some benefit to Canada-U.S. relations if these people had been formally informed or notified prior to seizure, giving them the opportunity of either declaring they had major repairs to be done on their boats or getting the boats out of the country. These people are now faced with a Canadian assessment and double taxation before they can take their boats back to the United States. This will amount to a great deal of money, and I suggest it makes about as much sense as the $8-tax this government recently put on American citizens flying into Canada or travelling on flights originating in Canada. That has to be the chippiest piece of legislation I have seen for a long time, but par for the course for this government.
I have remarked about the boating facilities on Kootenay Lake. I would like to be able to favourably remark on the fishing facilities as well. Unfortunately we are faced with another section of the Columbia River treaty; that final portion called the Kootenay River diversion. There is some question as to what impact that diversion will have on the Kootenay Lake fishery.
The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) has provided experts in their fields, such as limnolo-gists, to go into the Kootenay Lake area and carry out a careful study and analysis of the water quality of that lake. I wrote to the minister and asked him to provide me with a preliminary report on the water quality studies done by officials of his department-these experts whose qualifications I do not question. The Kootenay River diversion project is boiling and coming to a head. Public concern is really very
February 1, 1978

serious. What did the minister say to me in his reply? One of the most entertaining statements by the minister, which reflects Liberal thinking, was that he was not in a position to provide me with these figures, statistics and information at this time but would be pleased to do so in 1979.
The minister questions whether it was him who said that. Indeed, it was. The minister presupposes that he is going to be the minister of this department in 1979, and he also presupposes, which is even worse, that he will even be a minister in 1979. I suggest that is very much open to question and doubt.
This demonstrates the point that has been expressed by members of the opposition, that while the minister may be very sincere in what he says about the regulations and his dealings with the fishermen on the east and west coasts regarding the sort of fees that will be levied by the wharfingers, what guarantee do we have that the minister will be in place when those fees are established?
The minister is already in difficulty in respect of another piece of legislation. He declared that we had nothing to fear because he was in control. I refer to Bill C-38 which is far from settled. The minister knows that the province of British Columbia has not yet approved Bill C-38 or accepted its
Fishing and Recreational Harbours context. The minister knows that officials from various hydro projects across Canada where fisheries are involved have been to Ottawa expressing to his officials their concern over certain provisions of that bill which in effect could shut them down overnight. I suggest Ontario would have the biggest brown-out in its history.
The minister knows that the forest industry is far from satisfied. He knows also that the mining industry is far from satisfied and that there are other provinces in addition to British Columbia which have not yet accepted the legislation contained in Bill C-38.
I will grant the minister one victory. Let me compliment him on the stand he took with reference to the McGregor diversion. Clearly the province of British Columbia or, more appropriately, British Columbia Hydro, was fearful of the parasites in the water endemic to the Fraser moving into Arctic waterways, and there was no way to stop it. That was a major concern. The other major concern, spoken or unspoken, was that the federal government had expressed its very serious reservations about the McGregor diversion through the minister.
